title: Prevention and hindrance of performance
summary: A party’s interference with an event or performance it later invokes as a condition can affect its ability to rely on that event’s nonoccurrence.
notes:
McKenna examines the consequences of conduct affecting a certification requirement. The surrounding materials ask when one party’s obstruction, failure to cooperate, or control of a needed step excuses a condition or constitutes breach. Identify the promised cooperation, the actual interference, and the causal connection to the missing event.

The doctrine does not eliminate every condition merely because one party could influence it. The agreement may allocate relevant risks or discretion. Interpretation and good faith therefore remain important in deciding which actions the parties were entitled to take.

textbookImport.basis: Plain-language synthesis of the cited casebook passages; subject to the jurisdictional and source limits stated there.

topics.conditions: A party’s interference may change the consequence of a condition’s failure.
topics.good-faith: Promised cooperation and proper exercise of control matter.
